# Chapter 1: Introduction

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Applied mathematics is the process of applying mathematics to real world problems, and also learning and developing mathematical tools to solve these problems. Many of the advances in mathematics, such as in calculus, differential equations, vector calculus, Fourier analysis (which you will cover in the Second Year), computation and geometry have come directly from studying such applications. All mathematical descriptions of the real world are to a certain extent an approximation to the truth, but it is quite remarkable how (unreasonably effective) abstract mathematics is at representing the world that we live in, and allowing us to make predictions about how things will behave. When it comes to telling the future Mystic Meg is nothing compared to an applied mathematician. Some mathematicians can give the impression that applied maths is easy, just a matter of applying well known ideas in a routine way to solve routine problems. Nothing could be further from the truth! Firstly, the process of understanding how to describe the world in mathematical terms, and to then interpret the answers in a meaningful way, is very subtle (indeed) and is a skill which we will be teaching you in many of the courses that you will meet at Bath. We will call this process *mathematical modelling*. Secondly, the mathematics that we will use is far from trivial. Often the (for example nonlinear differential) equations that are used to represent reality are very hard to solve, and we need to use a great variety of mathematical techniques to make any progress. I assure you that the mathematics that you will be using in this, and future applied maths courses, is every bit as challenging as the maths that you will meet in all of you other courses. To quote the great Richard Feynmann you have to *think real hard* to do applied mathematics. Thirdly, and wonderfully, it is worth it. The mathematics that you will learn really does tell us what the world is doing, and often reveals surprising truths about the way that things work. If you don't believe me, watch the film *Hidden Figures* which will show you how a bunch of (female) mathematicians got us to the moon, and in the film *Apollo 13* how they got us back again.

The best way to do applied maths is to get a firm mathematical foundation to start with. This course develops the theory of *vectors* -- a major mathematical tool for modelling and analysis of various \`\`real world'' (physical, mechanical etc.) applications.

Vectors have numerous other applications too, for example, in electromagnetic waves which are important in the design of mobile phones, weather and climate forecasting, the design of industrial processes, personality tests and much more besides.



We will then combine our understanding of vetors with the main tools of calculus such as integration, differentiation and differential equations. Having done this we can then look at problems in kinematics and mechanics. *Kinematics* is the study of how bodies move. *Mechanics* deals with the action of forces on bodies and includes both statics and the study of motion. We shall consider \emph{Newtonian Mechanics}, including,

-   the motion of the planets and satellites,
-   projectiles (including a certain drop goal)
-   circular orbits
-   Some sporting problems

All of these will be illustrated by examples, some of which will involve some practical demonstrations in the lecture. You will also learn the general process of how to approach mathematically modelling a real life situation. In the 19th Century it was thought that Newtonian Mechanics was a well understood and rather dry subject, and that everything was very predictable. We now know that this is far from the case. For example the discovery of **chaos** which I will demonstrate in the lectures, shows that systems governed by Newtonian mechanics can have very bizzare behaviour indeed. In addition, a thorough understanding of mechanics is now *essential* for a career in computer animation with companies such as Pixar, and also in many areas of sport, as well as the space programme. It is also an essential part of the training of pilots, air traffic controllers, forensic scientists (think high speed cars, or bullets) and, as we shall see, in the design of pedestrian crossings, saving the whales and curing cancer!. Be prepared to be both amazed by this course, and highly employable at the end.

# Chapter 2: Vectors and the dot and cross product. 

------------------------------------------------------------------------

\noindent Before looking at the applications we need to understand the tools, namely vectors, and so the first few sections are about \emph{Vector Algebra} and then \emph{Vector Calculus}.

### 2.1 Introduction to Vector Algebra

Some quantities in mechanics, physics, or indeed life in general, are characterised by a *single real number*, for example, mass, density, temperature. However other physical quantities require the specification of both a *magnitude* and *direction*, for example, velocity, an acceleration, or a force. 

\noindent We shall assume that we live in a 3-Dimensional world which is part of a (3-D) Euclidean Space $R^3$, and for this course, vectors are 3-Dimensional. This means that a typical 3-dimensional vector ${\mathbf a} = (x,y,z)$ needs three values to specify it exactly. To give a precise mathematical definition we adopt the axioms of Euclidean geometry, namely, *points, straight lines, planes, parallel lines, distance,*\~etc. We will then think of vectors as geometrical objects for the main. (Note that this is not the only way to think of a vector. Basically anything which requires several coordinates to specifiy it can be thought of as a vector. For example if I want to go shopping and buy \pounds $x$ of sugar, \pounds $y$ of rice, and \pounds $z$ of strawberries, then my shopping for the day can be summarised by the single vector ${\mathbf a} = (x,y,z).$ However, for most of this course we will stick to the geometric interpretation of a vector which is summarised as follows.)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Definition 2.1** A vector is a directed line segment (DLS) characterised by two *ordered points* in 3-D Euclidean space, $P$ and $Q$, and is visualised as an arrow joining $P$ to $Q$. $P$ is the \emph{initial} point and $Q$ is the *terminal* point. The vector is denoted $\overrightarrow{PQ}$.

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot11, out.width='30%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap="A vector as a directed line segment from the point $P$ to the point $Q$"}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig21.jpg")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

\noindent Every vector has a direction and a length associated with it:

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Definition 2.2** *Length*

> The length of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ is the *distance* between $P$ and $Q$, and is denoted by $\|\overrightarrow{PQ}\|$. Often we say $\|{\overrightarrow{PQ}}\|$ is the *norm* of $\overrightarrow{PQ}$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Definition 2.3** *The Zero Vector*

> If $P$ and $Q$ coincide (that is $P = Q$) then the vector is called the zero segment (or zero vector), and is denoted by, ${\mathbf 0}$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From the Euclidean distance axioms, namely, (a) the distance from a point to itself is zero, and (b) the distance between any two distinct points is strictly positive, we have the following \`\`obvious'' result.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Proposition 2.4** $\overrightarrow{PQ} = {\mathbf 0} \iff \|{\overrightarrow{PQ}}\|= 0$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Proof**: $\overrightarrow{PQ} = {\mathbf 0}  \iff P=Q \iff \|\overrightarrow{PQ}\|=0.$ $\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Definition 2.5** Two directed line segments (DLSs) $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and \>$\overrightarrow{RS}$ are said to be **parallel** (or collinear) if they lie on parallel straight lines 1 and 2. The zero segment is regarded as being parallel to any vector.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

An important idea is that two DLSs which have the same direction and magnitude are `equal'' or`equivalent'', and we do not distinguish between them. This leads to the following definition.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Definition 2.6**

> Two DLSs $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and $\overrightarrow{RS}$ are said to be *equal* (or *equivalent*), that is, $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{RS}$, if

> -   They are colinear.
> -   They have the same magnitude, that is, $\|\overrightarrow{PQ}\| =
>     \| \overrightarrow{RS}\|$
> -   They point in the same direction.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Note that this definition doesn't mention the initial point of a DLS, so a DLS can be \`\`freely'' moved, in that, for any DLS $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ and for any other point $R$, there exists an equal (and unique) DLS with initial point at $R$. Note that all zero DLSs are regarded as being equivalent.

**Notation** It is convenient to have a single label to describe this, for example, $${\mathbf a} = \overrightarrow{PQ} = \overrightarrow{RS},$$

\noindent indicating that we don't distinguish between two equivalent DLSs. Hence, ${\mathbf a}$ represents a \`\`class'' of equivalent DLS's each with the same magnitude and direction as $\overrightarrow{PQ}$.

\noindent Finally, $\|{\mathbf a}\|$ will denote the length of the vector ${\mathbf a}$.

\noindent We will see presently that we can represent ${\mathbf a}$ as ${\mathbf a} = (a_1,a_2,a_3)$ and that $$\| {\mathbf a} \| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}.$$

### 2.2 Basic operations with vectors

\noindent In physical problems we often need to evaluate the combined effect of two processes characterised by two vectors, say ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$. In particular we will want to be able to add vectors, multiply vectors, and multiply them by scalars. This leads us to the first basic operation, namely, *addition* of two vectors.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Example:** The wind is blowing with velocity ${\mathbf a}$. A bird is flying with velocity ${\mathbf b}$ with respect to the air. What is the velocity, say ${\mathbf c}$, of the bird with respect to an observer on the ground. (As usual the \`velocity' is defined to be the change in position (displacement) per unit of time.)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Answer** The answer is simply that ${\mathbf c} = {\mathbf a} + {\mathbf b}$.

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot22, out.width='30%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap="*A bird flying into the wind*"}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig22.jpg")
```

\noindent This example motivates the following definition:

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Definition 2.7** *Vector addition* Given two vectors ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$. Position the vector ${\mathbf b}$ so that its initial point coincides with the terminal point of ${\mathbf a}$. Then ${\mathbf c} = {\mathbf a} + {\mathbf b}$ is defined by the DLS whose initial point coincides with the initial point of ${\mathbf a}$ and whose terminal point coincides with the terminal point of ${\mathbf b}$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Exercise:** Check that this definition is consistent with the following equivalences. If $$
\overrightarrow{P_1Q_1}\; = \;\overrightarrow{P_2Q_2}\; , \;
\overrightarrow{Q_1S_1} = \overrightarrow{Q_2S_2}
$$ then we need to show that $$
\overrightarrow{P_1Q_1} +
\overrightarrow{Q_1S_1}\;=\;\overrightarrow{P_2Q_2} +
\overrightarrow{Q_2S_2}.
$$

**Property 1:** *Commutativity of addition:* ${\mathbf a}
+ {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf b} + {\mathbf a}$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Proof:** Let ${\mathbf a} = \overrightarrow{PQ},\; {\mathbf b} = \overrightarrow{PR}$. Construct the parallelogram $PQSR$ (see diagram).

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot23, out.width='30%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig23.jpg")
```

Then, from the definition of equivalence of vectors, and the properties of parallelograms $$
\overrightarrow{RS}= \overrightarrow{PQ}={\mathbf a}, \quad \overrightarrow{QS}= \overrightarrow{PR}= {\mathbf b}.
$$

Thus, from the definition of addition, $\overrightarrow{PQ}+\overrightarrow{QS}=\overrightarrow{PS}$, or $$
 {\mathbf a} + {\mathbf b} =: {\mathbf c}.
$$ On the other hand,

$$\overrightarrow{PR} + \overrightarrow{RS} \; =\; \overrightarrow{PS} \; = \; {\mathbf c}
$$ and so $$
{\mathbf b} + {\mathbf a} = {\mathbf c}$$ Hence, $$
{\mathbf a} + {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf b} + {\mathbf a} \quad \forall \quad {\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}.
$$

**Property 2** *Associativity of addition:* Let ${\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}$ and ${\mathbf c}$ be three vectors. Then $$
({\mathbf a} + {\mathbf b}) + {\mathbf c} = {\mathbf a} + ({\mathbf b} + {\mathbf c}).
$$ (See Tutorial Sheet 1, Question 2).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Property 3** *The zero vector:* Consider a zero segment, namely, $\overrightarrow{PP}$. All zero segments are regarded as equivalent and we write $$
\overrightarrow{PP}\;=\;\overrightarrow{QQ}\;=\;{\mathbf 0}.
$$ Since by definition $$
\overrightarrow{PQ} + \overrightarrow{QQ}\;=\; \overrightarrow{PQ} \;=\;\overrightarrow{PP} +
\overrightarrow{PQ},
$$ it follows that $$
{\mathbf a} + {\mathbf 0} =  {\mathbf a} = {\mathbf 0} + {\mathbf a}.
$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Property 4** *Negation of vectors:* Given a vector ${\mathbf a} = \overrightarrow{PQ}$ we denote the **negative** of ${\mathbf a}$ by $-{\mathbf a}$, and define it by reversing its direction, so that, $$
-{\mathbf a} = \overrightarrow{QP}.
$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Then, clearly, $$
{\mathbf a} + (-{\mathbf a}) = \overrightarrow{PQ} + \overrightarrow{QP} = \overrightarrow{PP} = {\mathbf 0}.
$$ and so $$
{\mathbf a} +(-{\mathbf a}) = {\mathbf 0}.
$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Definition 2.8** *Subtraction*

> $${\mathbf a} - {\mathbf b} \, \equiv {\mathbf a} + (-{\mathbf{b}}).$$

To show this consider the paralollogram below

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot24, out.width='30%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig24.jpg")
```

If ${\mathbf a} = \overrightarrow{PQ}$ and ${\mathbf b} = \overrightarrow{PR}$, then $$
{\mathbf a} - {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf a} + (-{\mathbf b}) = \overrightarrow{PQ}+ \overrightarrow{QT} = \overrightarrow{PT}. 
$$

\noindent Now, since $PRQT$ is a parallelogram, $\overrightarrow{PT} =\overrightarrow{RQ}$ and hence $\overrightarrow{RQ}=  {\mathbf a}-{\mathbf b}$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### Fun stuff

The eagle eyed amongst you will have noticed that the *set* of vectors is closed under the operation of addition, that addition is associative, it has a zero element, and it has inverses.

Therefore the set of vectors with addition is an example of an *abelian group*. So we are able to use results from the Algebra courses to help us to study vectors. In fact vectors are not only a group they have further properties which make them into (you guessed it) a *vector space*.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

This extra property is that of *multiplication by a scalar* or *scalar multiplication*.

Consider ${\mathbf a} + {\mathbf a}$. It is natural to write ${\mathbf a} + {\mathbf a} = 2{\mathbf a}$. The vector $2{\mathbf a}$ has the *same direction* as ${\mathbf a}$ but it is *twice as long*: $$\|2 {\mathbf a}\| \;=\;2 \|{\mathbf a}\|.$$

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot25, out.width='30%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig25.jpg")
```

On the other hand, it is natural to write $$
-{\mathbf a} = (-1) {\mathbf a} \;,\;\overrightarrow{PS} = (-1) {\mathbf a}.
$$ Thus, multiplication by $-1$ results in altering the direction of a vector. This motivates the following definition of scalar multiplication.

> **Definition 2.9** *Scalar Multiplication*

> For any real number $\lambda$, the scalar multiplication of ${\mathbf a}$ by $\lambda$ produces the vector ${\mathbf b} \equiv \lambda {\mathbf a}$ such that

> -   ${\mathbf b}$ is collinear to ${\mathbf a}$,

> -   $\| {\mathbf b} \|  = |\lambda | \| {\mathbf a} \|$,

> -   ${\mathbf b}$ and ${\mathbf a}$ have the *same direction* if $\lambda >
>     0$, and opposite if $\lambda < 0$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Property 5:** *Associativity of scalar multiplication:* $\lambda(\mu {\mathbf a}) = (\lambda \mu)
{\mathbf a}$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Property 6:** *Distributivity of scalar multiplication with respect to addition of vectors:* $\lambda({\mathbf a} + {\mathbf b}) = \lambda {\mathbf a} +
\lambda {\mathbf b}.$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Property 7:** *Distributivity of scalar multiplication with respect to addition of scalars:}* $(\lambda + \mu) {\mathbf a} = \lambda {\mathbf a} + \mu {\mathbf a}$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Property 8:** $1 \cdot {\mathbf a} = {\mathbf a}$

(Properties 5 - 8 can be directly derived from the above definitions.)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Student Exercises:**

-   [a] Draw a figure to show that Property 6 is true. (Hint: Think similar triangles.)
-   [b] Give arguments to show that Property 5 and Property 7 are true.

**Advert** You should do these, and later student exercises! They are there to help make sure that you understand the material so far. If you have problems with them, then discuss these with your tutors.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Based on these properties we can now summarise the 'rules' that any set that claims to be a 'vector space' needs to obey

**Eight Rules of Vector Algebra (or Vector Arithmetic)**

-   ${\mathbf a} + {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf b} + {\mathbf a}$
-   $({\mathbf a} + {\mathbf b}) + {\mathbf c} = {\mathbf a} + ({\mathbf b} + {\mathbf c})$
-   ${\mathbf a} + {\mathbf 0} = {\mathbf 0} + {\mathbf a} = {\mathbf a}$
-   ${\mathbf a}+ (-{\mathbf a}) = {\mathbf 0}$
-   $\lambda (\mu {\mathbf a}) = (\lambda \mu) {\mathbf a}$
-   $\lambda ({\mathbf a}+ {\mathbf b}) = \lambda {\mathbf a} + \lambda {\mathbf b}$
-   $(\lambda + \mu) {\mathbf a} = \lambda {\mathbf a} + \mu {\mathbf a}$
-   $1 \cdot {\mathbf a} = {\mathbf a}$

These 8 properties are satisfied by directed line segments (with addition, negation and scalar multiplication introduced above). More generally, (1) - (8) may be regarded as \`\`Axioms'', and quantities that satisfy them are called **vectors**. The directed line segment is merely one example of an object satisfying (1) - (8). Other examples are matrices and functions, among others.

*Remark* Many physical quantities (e.g. velocity, force) are indeed vectors. However not **all** quantities having both a magnitude and a direction satisfy these rules. For example consider the operation of rotation: the axis of rotation gives the direction, the angle is the magnitude. Let \`\`addition'' be superposition of rotations. Then the commutative property does not hold.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.3 Unit vectors

> **Definition 2.10** A vector whose length is $1$ is called a unit vector. Given a non-zero vector ${\mathbf a}$, that is ${\mathbf a} \ne {\mathbf 0}$, the unit vector **in the direction of** ${\mathbf a}$ is

$$
\hat{{\mathbf a}} = \frac{1}{\|{\mathbf a}\|} {\mathbf a}.
$$

\noindent Check: $\|\hat{{\mathbf a}}\| = \left|\frac{1}{\|{\mathbf a}\|}\right|
\|{\mathbf a}\| = \frac{\|{\mathbf a}\|}{\|{\mathbf a}\|} = 1$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.4 Position Vectors

Position vectors are a way of identifying a *point* with a *vector*.

Let $O$ be the origin (which is a fixed point) in $R^3$. Any point $A$ can be identified with its **position vector** ${\mathbf a}$ by $$
{\mathbf a} := \overrightarrow{OA}.
$$

\noindent The main concept to remember here is that the initial point of any position vector is always the origin. It follows that for points $A$ and $B$ $$
\overrightarrow{AB} = \overrightarrow{AO} + \overrightarrow{OB} = \overrightarrow{OB} - \overrightarrow{OA} = {\mathbf b} - {\mathbf a}
$$

\noindent Position vectors are very useful for solving problems in geometry and mechanics.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Useful rules**

-   Let the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ be ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$ respectively. Then $\overrightarrow{AB} = {\mathbf b} - {\mathbf a}$

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot1a, out.width='30%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("ch1a.jpg")
```

-   Let $C$ be the *midpoint* of $AB$ and so ${\mathbf c}$ is the position vector of $\overrightarrow{OC}$. Therefore $${\mathbf c} = \overrightarrow{OA} + \overrightarrow{AC} = \overrightarrow{OA} + \frac{1}{2} \overrightarrow{AB} = {\mathbf a} + \frac{1}{2}({\mathbf b} - {\mathbf a}) = \frac{1}{2} ({\mathbf a} +
    {\mathbf b}).$$

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot1k, out.width='30%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("ch1k.jpg")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Now let's consider two examples.

**Example 1:** Assume that the vectors ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$ are non-zero and non-colinear (or non-parallel) and let $\lambda, \mu$ be real numbers. Then

$$\lambda {\mathbf a} +\mu {\mathbf b}= {\mathbf 0} \Rightarrow \lambda=0, \quad \mbox{and} \quad  \mu=0.
$$ **Proof** First, assume $\lambda \ne 0$. Then

$${\mathbf a} =-
\frac{\mu}{\lambda} {\mathbf b}$$

implying ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$ are parallel.

But ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$ are **not** parallel, so $\mu=0$, which implies ${\mathbf a}= {\mathbf 0}$.

This is a contradiction. Thus $\lambda=0.$ Hence

$$\mu {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf 0},$$ \noindent and since ${\mathbf b} \ne {\mathbf 0}$, we must have $\mu=0. \Box$

\*\* NOTE \*\* This hugely important result is called the **linear independence** of two non-parallel vectors.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

\noindent We will now look at a worked example, which is the sort of question that you might be faced with in your Summer exam. This example shows that position vectors are useful for solving geometry problems

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Worked example 2:** *Prove that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.*

**Answer:** **Always** start with a diagram.

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot1kk, out.width='50%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("ch1kk.jpg")
```

The diagonals of the parallelogram are:

$$\overrightarrow{AB} =  {\mathbf b} - {\mathbf a}$$ $$\overrightarrow{OC} = {\mathbf b} + {\mathbf a}$$

Let the diagonals intersect at the point $P$. So

$$\overrightarrow{AP}
= \lambda \overrightarrow{AB} = \lambda ({\mathbf b} - {\mathbf a}) \quad \mbox{for
some  $\lambda \in R$}$$ \mbox{and} $$\overrightarrow{OP} = \mu ({\mathbf b} + {\mathbf a}) \quad \mbox{for some  $\mu \in R$.}$$

\noindent To show that the diagonals bisect each other we need to show that $\lambda = \frac{1}{2}$, $\mu = \frac{1}{2}$. (Check that you understand why this must be so.)

Now

$$\overrightarrow{OP} = \overrightarrow{OA} + \overrightarrow{AB}$$ therefore $$\mu({\mathbf a} + {\mathbf b}) = {\mathbf a} + \lambda ({\mathbf b} - {\mathbf a})$$ So $$(1 - \mu - \lambda){\mathbf a} + (\lambda - \mu) {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf 0}.$$

\noindent Now, we make use of *linear independence*. From the previous result it follows that the coefficients of the vectors ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$ must **both** be zero. Hence $$ 1 - \mu - \lambda = 0 \quad \mbox{and} \quad  \lambda - \mu = 0. $$ Solving these two equations we see that $\lambda = \mu =
\frac{1}{2}.$ Hence the diagonals bisect each other. $\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.5 Vectors in Cartesian coordinates

Although vectors are entities in their own right and it is useful for many applications to treat them in this way (also this is how Matlab works with vectors), treating them within a coordinate system is often very useful for actual calculations.

To do this in three-dimensional Euclidean space we introduce a right-handed mutually orthogonal coordinate frame ($Oxyz$) with origin $O$, and with coordinate planes $Oxy,Oyz$ and $Ozx$. See diagram following.

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot1c1b, out.width='60%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("ch1b.jpg")
```

\noindent In general, three non-zero vectors ${\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}, {\mathbf c}$ (which have the same initial point and are not coplanar) form a *right-handed co-ordinate system*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

A **very important set of vectors** are ${\mathbf i}, {\mathbf j}$ and ${\mathbf k}$. These are the unit vectors pointing in the positive directions of $Ox, Oy, Oz$ respectively. Let ${\mathbf a}$ be an arbitrary vector. We can always decompose ${\mathbf a}$ into a *linear combination* of ${\mathbf i}, {\mathbf j}, {\mathbf k}$ as follows.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Proposition 2.11**

> Any vector ${\mathbf a}$, has components $a_1, a_2, a_3 \in R$ such that ${\mathbf a} = a_1 {\mathbf i} + a_2 {\mathbf j} + a_3 {\mathbf k}$. The values \>of the components $a_1, a_2, a_3$ are {\em unique}.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Definition 2.12** The values $a_1, a_2, a_3$ are called the **components** of ${\mathbf a}$, and we write ${\mathbf a} = (a_1, a_2, a_3)$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Proof:** In part (1) we prove existence, and then in part (2) we show uniqueness.

-   **Existence** (geometrical):

Let $A$ be a point such that ${\mathbf a} = \overrightarrow{OA}$. Construct a \`\`box'' (a rectangular parallelepiped) with faces parallel to the coordinate planes as illustrated below

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot1m, out.width='30%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("ch1m.jpg")
```

Now let ${\mathbf a} = \overrightarrow{OA}$. Now ${\mathbf a} = \overrightarrow{OA} = \overrightarrow{OB} + \overrightarrow{BC} + \overrightarrow{CA}$, and since $\overrightarrow{OB}$ is parallel to the unit vector ${\mathbf i}$, there exists a value $a_1$ such that $\overrightarrow{OB} = a_1 {\mathbf i}$. Similarly $\overrightarrow{BC} = a_2 {\mathbf j},$ and $\overrightarrow{CA} = a_3 {\mathbf k}$. Therefore $$
{\mathbf a} = a_1 {\mathbf i} + a_2 {\mathbf j} + a_3 {\mathbf k}.
$$

-   **Uniqueness** (algebraic):

Assume there exists another representation $$
{\mathbf a} = a_1' \;  {\mathbf i} + a_2' \; {\mathbf j} + a_3' \; {\mathbf k},
$$ for some real numbers $a_1',a_2',a_3'$. Subtracting gives $$
(a_1 - a_1') \; {\mathbf i} + (a_2 - a_2') \; {\mathbf j} + (a_3 - a_3') \; {\mathbf k} = {\mathbf 0}.
$$ Assume, without loss of generality, that $a_1 \ne a_1'$. Then $$
 {\mathbf i}  = -\,\frac{a_2 -
a_2'}{a_1 - a_1'} \; {\mathbf j} -\,\frac{a_3 - a_3'}{a_1 - a_1'}\;  {\mathbf k}.
$$ Therefore ${\mathbf i}$ is *co-planar* to ${\mathbf j}$ and ${\mathbf k}$ (i.e. ${\mathbf i}$ lies in same plane as ${\mathbf j}$ & ${\mathbf k}$). But ${\mathbf i}$ is *orthogonal* to the $Oyz$ plane, which is a contradiction. $\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### **Examples of the use of components:**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Length**

> $$ \|{\mathbf a} \| = (a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2)^{\frac{1}{2}}$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We obtain this **hugely important**, and useful, result by applying Pythagoras' theorem twice:

$$\|{\mathbf a} \|^2=\|\overrightarrow{OA}\|^2=\|\overrightarrow{OC}\|^2+\|\overrightarrow{CA}\|^2=\left(\|\overrightarrow{OB}\|^2+\|\overrightarrow{BC}\|^2\right)+
\|\overrightarrow{CA}\|^2=
a_1^2 + a_2^2 +a_3^2. 
$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Addition:**

$$
{\mathbf a} + {\mathbf b} = (a_1 \; {\mathbf i} + a_2 \;  {\mathbf j}  + a_3 \; {\mathbf k}) + (b_1 \; {\mathbf i}
+ b_2 \; {\mathbf j} + b_3 \; {\mathbf k})
$$

$$
 = (a_1 + b_1) \; {\mathbf i} + (a_2 + b_2) \; {\mathbf j} +
(a_3 + b_3) \; {\mathbf k}
$$

$$
= (a_1 + b_1, a_2 + b_2, a_3 + b_3).  \quad \quad  (*)
$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Multiplication by scalar:**

$$
\lambda {\mathbf a} = \lambda (a_1 \; {\mathbf i} + a_2 \; {\mathbf j} + a_3 \; {\mathbf k}) =
(\lambda a_1) \; {\mathbf i} + (\lambda a_2) \; {\mathbf j} + (\lambda a_3) \; {\mathbf k} =
(\lambda a_1, \lambda a_2, \lambda a_3). \quad \quad (**)
$$

**Exercise:** Which of the laws of vector algebra have been used in (\*) and (\*\*) above?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.6 The dot (or scalar) product.

Having looked how we can add two vectors, we will now look at how to multiply them. There are essentially two ways to do this. The **scalar product**, which produces a scalar (a number) and the **vector product** which produces a vector. We will need to learn about both of these.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Definition 2.13** Given two vectors ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$, their **dot** or **scalar** product, denoted by ${\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b}$) is a scalar defined by

> $$
> {\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b} = \left\{
> \begin{array}{ll}
> \|{\mathbf a}\|\|{\mathbf b}\| \cos(\theta), &\mbox{if } {\mathbf a} \ne {\mathbf 0} \mbox{ and }
> {\mathbf b} \ne {\mathbf 0}\\
> 0\;\;\; ,&\mbox{if } {\mathbf a} = {\mathbf 0} \mbox{ or } {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf 0},
> \end{array}\right.
> $$ where $\theta$ is the angle between ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$ ($0 \le \theta \le
> \pi$).

Note that as $\cos(\theta) = \cos(-\theta)$ it doesn't matter what the orientation of the angle is.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

For ${\mathbf a} \ne {\mathbf 0}, {\mathbf b} \ne {\mathbf 0}$, we have

$$\cos(\theta) = \frac{ {\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b}}{ \|{\mathbf a}\| \; \|{\mathbf b}\|},
$$ and so the dot product tells us about the **angle** between two vectors.

If ${\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b} =0$, then ${\mathbf a}$ is *orthogonal* (perpendicular) to ${\mathbf b}$.

The converse is also true, so we have the **hugely important result** that:

Two non-zero vectors ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$ are **orthogonal** if and only if ${\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b} = 0$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The dot product is an **insanely useful concept**. It will be used extensively as a mathematical tool in the manipulation of vectors. However it also has meaning in many physical situations, for example, if ${\mathbf a}$ represents a *force* and ${\mathbf b}$ represents a *displacement*, then $W = {\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b}$ is the *work done (the energy used) by the force*. We will use this ide a lot in the mechanics part of this course.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**The component (or *algebraic*) form of the dot product**

From the cosine rule

$$ \|{\mathbf a} - {\mathbf b}\|^2 = \|{\mathbf a}\|^2 + \|{\mathbf b}\|^2 -
2 \; \|{\mathbf a}\|\;\|{\mathbf b}\|\cos(\theta) =\|{\mathbf a}\|^2 + \|{\mathbf b}\|^2 -
2 \; {\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b}
$$ 
Therefore, 



$${\mathbf a}. {\mathbf b} = \frac{1}{2}\left(\|{\mathbf a} \|^2 +
\|{\mathbf b}\|^2 - \|{\mathbf a}- {\mathbf b}\|^2\right) 
= \frac{1}{2} \left(a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2
+ b_1^2 + b_2^2 + b_3^2 - (a_1 - b_1)^2 - (a_2 - b_2)^2 - (a_3 -
b_3)^2\right) = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3
$$

Thus we have the really **very very** important result

$${\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b} = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3.$$

**Note** that we define the dot product here in a geometric manner and then deduce the component form.

Anton does the reverse - the dot product is defined in Def 12.3.1 and then the geometric form is deduced in Theorem 12.3.3. Matlab defines the dot product in the same way as Anton.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Properties of the dot product:**

Given the vectors ${\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}, {\mathbf c}$ and for any scalar $\lambda$:

-   ${\mathbf a}. {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf b}.{\mathbf a}$
-   ${\mathbf a}. ({\mathbf b} + {\mathbf c}) = {\mathbf a}. {\mathbf b} + {\mathbf a}. {\mathbf c}$
-   $\lambda ({\mathbf a}. {\mathbf b}) = (\lambda {\mathbf a}). {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf a}. (\lambda {\mathbf b})$
-   ${\mathbf a}. {\mathbf a} = \| {\mathbf a} \|^2$
-   ${\mathbf a}. {\mathbf  0} = 0$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Remark** These properties can also be used as axioms in an abstract theory of vectors. If we proceed along this line, then we first define a \`\`Linear Space'' using the addition and scalar multiplication properties we've seen before, and then introduce an *inner product* based on the rules for the dot product. You'll meet all this in later courses. For example the theory of *Hilbert Spaces* is developed from these considerations, and this theory is essential in the study of Quantum Mechanics.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Student Exercise** (you know what to do!):

-   [a] Derive (1) and (4) from the geometrical definition of the dot product.
-   [b] Derive (2) and (3) from the component form of the dot product.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The dot product is used frequently when solving problems, such as those you will meet in your exam. Here are some examples.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Example 1 (From Part A of a recent exam):** (Finding the angle between two vectors) Let ${\mathbf a} = 2 \; {\mathbf i} - {\mathbf j} + {\mathbf k},$ and ${\mathbf b} =
{\mathbf i} + {\mathbf j} + 2 {\mathbf k}$. Find the angle $\theta$ between ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$.

**Answer** We know that $$\cos(\theta) = \frac{{\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b}}{ \|{\mathbf a}\| \|{\mathbf b} \|}.$$ Now, from the component formula for ${\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b}$ we have, $${\mathbf a}. {\mathbf b} = 2 \times 1 + (-1) \times  1 + 1
\times 2 =3$$ and $$\|{\mathbf a} \| = (2^2 + (-1)^2 + 1^2)^{\frac{1}{2}} =
\sqrt{6}, \quad \|{\mathbf b}\| = (1^2 + 1^2 + 2^2)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{6}.$$ It follows that $$\cos(\theta) = \frac{{\mathbf a}. {\mathbf b}}{\|{\mathbf a}\|
\cdot \|{\mathbf b}\|} = \frac{3}{\sqrt{6} \cdot  \sqrt{6}} =
\frac{1}{2},$$ therefore $\theta = \frac{\pi}{3}$ (in radians)

**Exercise** What is the angle in degrees?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Example 2:** The dot product provides an easy way of finding components of vectors. For example, if $$
{\mathbf a} = (a_{1},a_{2},a_{3}) = a_{1} \; {\mathbf i} + a_{2} \; {\mathbf j} + a_{3} \; {\mathbf k}
$$ then $$
{\mathbf a} . {\mathbf i} = a_{1}, \quad \mbox{the component of} \quad  {\mathbf a} 
\quad \mbox{in the
direction of} \quad  {\mathbf i}.
$$ For the *basis* vectors ${\mathbf i}, {\mathbf j},
{\mathbf k}$ we have $$
{\mathbf i}.{\mathbf i} = {\mathbf j}.{\mathbf j} = {\mathbf k}.{\mathbf k} =
1, \quad {\mathbf i}.{\mathbf j} = {\mathbf j}.{\mathbf k} = {\mathbf k}.{\mathbf i} = 0.
$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Example 3** This is an example of a use of the dot product to do quite a clever piece of geometry.

Find the angle between a diagonal of a cube and one of its edges.

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot1w, out.width='30%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("ch1w.jpg")
```

**Solution** Consider a cube of size $d$, let ${\mathbf a}=\overrightarrow{OA}$ be the diagonal and let ${\mathbf b}=\overrightarrow{OB}$.

$${\mathbf a} = \overrightarrow{OA}
= d \; {\mathbf i} + d \; {\mathbf j} + d \; {\mathbf k} 
=  (d,d,d) $$ $$ {\mathbf b} = \overrightarrow{OB} = d \; {\mathbf i} =  (d,0,0).$$ $$\cos(\theta) = \frac{{\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b}}{\|{\mathbf a}\|\|{\mathbf b}\|} =
\frac{d^2}{\sqrt{3}d.d} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$$ Therefore $$\theta =\cos^{-1} \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right).$$ $\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Beware** A common error is to say: If ${\mathbf x} . {\mathbf a} = {\mathbf x}. {\mathbf b}$ then ${\mathbf a} = {\mathbf b}$ 

This is clearly incorrect. The correct reasoning goes as follows:

If ${\mathbf x} . {\mathbf a} = {\mathbf x}. {\mathbf b}$ then ${\mathbf x}. ({\mathbf a}-{\mathbf b})= 0$. Thus ${\mathbf x}$ is orthogonal to $({\mathbf a}-{\mathbf b})$ .

However, we have a useful Lemma and Corollary, where the key phrase in both is **for all** ${\mathbf x}$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Lemma 2.14** If ${\mathbf x}.{\mathbf c} =0$ **for all** ${\mathbf x}$, then ${\mathbf c} = {\mathbf 0}.$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Proof** Take ${\mathbf x}={\mathbf c}$. Then ${\mathbf c}.{\mathbf c}=0$, so $\| {\mathbf c} \|^2=0
\Rightarrow {\mathbf c}={\mathbf 0}. \Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Corollary 2.15** If ${\mathbf x}.{\mathbf a}={\mathbf x}.{\mathbf b}$ for all ${\mathbf x}$, then ${\mathbf a} = {\mathbf b}$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Proof** Rearranging gives ${\mathbf x}.({\mathbf a} - {\mathbf b})=0$ for all ${\mathbf x}$, and using Lemma 2.14, we have ${\mathbf a}-{\mathbf b}={\mathbf 0} \Rightarrow {\mathbf a}={\mathbf b}. \Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Exercise**\* Why is Corollary 2.15 different from the Beware example?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Orthogonal projection

Consider a vector ${\mathbf a} \ne {\mathbf 0}$ and ${\mathbf b}$. A useful way to represent ${\mathbf b}$ is in the form: $$
{\mathbf b} = {\mathbf b}_{||} + {\mathbf b}_\bot,
$$ where ${\mathbf b}_{||}$ is parallel to ${\mathbf a}$, and ${\mathbf b}_\bot$ is orthogonal to ${\mathbf a}$, so that ${\mathbf a}.{\mathbf b}_\bot=0$. (See diagram.)

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot26, out.width='40%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig26.jpg")
```

To show this we let $${\mathbf b}_{||} = \lambda {\mathbf a},$$ for some real number $\lambda$. Therefore, \begin{eqnarray*}
{\mathbf b}. {\mathbf a} & =& ({\mathbf b}_{||} + {\mathbf b}_\bot). {\mathbf a}\\
 & =& ({\mathbf b}_{||}). {\mathbf a}\\
 & = & \lambda {\mathbf a}. {\mathbf a}\\
 & =& \lambda \|{\mathbf a}\|^2.
\end{eqnarray*} Hence, since ${\mathbf a} \ne {\mathbf 0}$, $$\lambda = \frac{{\mathbf b}. {\mathbf a}}{\|{\mathbf a}\|^2}$$ and so we can determine ${\mathbf b}_{||}$. Next, ${\mathbf b}_\bot$ can be found from the equation ${\mathbf b}_\bot = {\mathbf b} - {\mathbf b}_{||}$. Thus,

$$
{\mathbf b}_{||} = \frac{({\mathbf b}.{\mathbf a})}{\|{\mathbf a \|^2}} {\mathbf a}, \quad \quad
{\mathbf b}_\bot = {\mathbf b} - \frac{({\mathbf b}.{\mathbf a})}{\|{\mathbf a}\|^2} {\mathbf a}.$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.7 The cross (or vector) product

The cross product gives us a way of *multiplying* two vectors to give another vector. It was invented in the 19th Century by the great French mathematician Lagrange and has proved a vital tool for vector calculus ever since.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Often in applications one needs to find a vector orthogonal to two other vectors. This is accomplished using the cross product. However the cross product has many other uses, for example in computer graphics, mechanics, weather forecasting, electromagnetism, physics, and geometry.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot27, out.width='40%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig27.jpg")
```

> **Definition 2.16** Given two vectors ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$,which are at an angle $\theta$ apart, their **cross** or **vector** product ${\mathbf c}$ denoted by ${\mathbf c} = {\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}$ is a vector which

> -   [i] is orthogonal to both ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$
> -   [ii] $\|{\mathbf c}\| = \|{\mathbf a}\|\;\|{\mathbf b}\| \sin(\theta), \quad (0 \le
>     \theta \le \pi)$
> -   [iii] If ${\mathbf a}\; \| \; {\mathbf b}$, then ${\mathbf a} \times
>     {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf 0}$. Otherwise, the direction of ${\mathbf c}$ is such that ${\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}, {\mathbf c}$ form a right-handed system (that is, all the angles are less than $\pi$).

------------------------------------------------------------------------


**IMPORTANT NOTE, PLEASE READ** In some older text books, exam questions for versions of this course, and possibly at school, you may have seen the notation ${\mathbf c} = {\mathbf a} \wedge {\mathbf b}$ for the cross product. In these notes I will follow the more usual practice now of using ${\mathbf c} = {\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}$. However, these two notations mean exactly the same thing.

For this course please use the ${\mathbf c} = {\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}$ notation for **all** of your work.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

As well as its numerous applications in geometry (such as calculating volumes and areas), the cross product plays a **VERY** important role in mechanics, especially when rotation is involved. We shall see many examples of this. For example the angular momentum of a body, and the torque/couple generated by a force are all expressed in terms of the cross product. The Coriolis and Magnus forces forces experienced by a spinning body in motion (think of the Earths atmosphere or a football), and the Lorentz force $\mathbf{F}$ experienced by an electron of charge $e$ moving at velocity $\mathbf{v}$ in a magnetic field $\mathbf{B}$ is given by $$\mathbf{F} = e \; \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B}.$$ When coupled to the *gradient* operator $\nabla$, which we will meet later in this course, we get the *curl* operator $\nabla \times$ which allows us to define quantities such as vorticity (which is vital for weather forecasting) and links electricity and magnetism together in Maxwell's equations.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

As advertised above, there is a simple **geometrical interpretation** of the length of a cross product in terms of an **area**. First, note that $\|{\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}\| =
 \| {\mathbf a} \| \| {\mathbf b} \| \sin(\theta) = \| {\mathbf a}\|\;\|{\mathbf b}_\bot \|$, since $\|{\mathbf b}_\bot\|=\|{\mathbf b}\|  \sin(\theta)$. Thus the length of $\|{\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b} \|$ equals the area of the parallelogram generated by ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$.

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot28, out.width='40%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig28.jpg")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Lemma 2.17**

> -   [1] ${\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b} = -{\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf a}$ So the cross product is **not** commutative. In fact it is **anti-commutative**.
> -   [2] ${\mathbf a} \times ({\mathbf b} + {\mathbf c}) = ({\mathbf a}  \times {\mathbf b} +
>     ({\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf c})$
> -   [3] $\lambda ({\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}) = (\lambda {\mathbf a}) \times
>     {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf a} \times (\lambda {\mathbf b})$
> -   [4] ${\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf a} = {\mathbf 0}, \forall
>     {\mathbf a}\;\quad (\mbox{since}\;\sin(\theta) = 0).$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Proof of [1]:** Firstly, ${\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}$ and ${\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf a}$ are both orthogonal to ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$: so they are parallel.

Next, $$\|{\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}\| = \|{\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf a}\| = \|{\mathbf a}\| \|{\mathbf b}\| \sin(\theta)$$ so that ${\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}$ and ${\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf a}$ have the same magnitude. Finally, ${\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}$ form a right handed system.Thus ${\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}$ is in the opposite direction to ${\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf a}$ and so, $$
 {\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b} = -{\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf a} \,.
$$ $\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Proof of (2):** We'll delay the proof of this till after we introduce the *scalar triple product*. (Historical Note: I was asked this question in my Cambridge Entrance exam.)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Important examples:**

$${\mathbf i} \times {\mathbf i} = {\mathbf j} \times {\mathbf j} = {\mathbf k} \times {\mathbf k} = {\mathbf 0}. $$ $${\mathbf i} \times {\mathbf j} = {\mathbf k}, \quad {\mathbf j} \times {\mathbf k} = {\mathbf i}, \quad {\mathbf k} \times {\mathbf i} = {\mathbf j}.$$ $${\mathbf j}\times {\mathbf i} = -{\mathbf k},  \quad {\mathbf k} \times {\mathbf j} = -{\mathbf i}, \quad {\mathbf i} \times {\mathbf k} = -{\mathbf j}.$$

(Proofs from the definition.)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**The component form of the vector product:** This is a bit messy, but it is an important way to calculate the cross product. The best way to remember this is to use the 'determinant' method which we will come on to shortly Given two vectors

$${\mathbf a} = a_1 \; {\mathbf i} + a_2 \;{\mathbf j} + a_3 \;{\mathbf k}
 \quad \mbox{and} \quad {\mathbf b} = b_1 \;{\mathbf i} + b_2 \;{\mathbf j} + b_3 \; {\mathbf k}
$$ then (learn this, you are **expected** to know it for your examination!!!)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> $$ {\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b} = (a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2)\; {\mathbf i} + (a_3 b_1 - a_1 b_3) \; {\mathbf j} + (a_1 b_2 - a_2 b_1) \; {\mathbf k} \; \; $$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We establish this by using the rules for the cross products of the unit vectors as follows. $$
{\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b} = (a_1 {\mathbf i} + a_2 {\mathbf j} + a_3 {\mathbf k})\times( b_1 {\mathbf i} + b_2{\mathbf j} + b_3 {\mathbf k}) $$ $$ = a_1 b_1 {\mathbf i} \times {\mathbf i} + a_1 b_2 {\mathbf i} \times {\mathbf j} + a_1 b_3 {\mathbf i}\times {\mathbf k}$$ $$+a_2 b_1 {\mathbf j} \times {\mathbf i} + a_2 b_2 {\mathbf j} \times {\mathbf j} + a_2 b_3 {\mathbf j} \times {\mathbf k} + $$ $$ a_3 b_1 {\mathbf k} \times {\mathbf i} + a_3 b_2 {\mathbf k} \times {\mathbf j} + a_3 b_3 {\mathbf k}
\times {\mathbf k} $$ $$= a_1 b_2 {\mathbf k} - a_1 b_3 {\mathbf j} - a_2 b_1 {\mathbf k} + a_2 b_3 {\mathbf i} + a_3 b_1 {\mathbf j} - a_3 b_2 {\mathbf i} $$ $$ = (a_2 b_3 - a_3 b_2) {\mathbf i} + (a_3 b_1 - a_1 b_3) {\mathbf j} + (a_1 b_2 - a_2
b_1) {\mathbf k}. $$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

There is a convenient way of calculating, and remembering, the vector product using $3 \times 3$ determinants which you will also meet in the algebra courses. This is how I remember the formula myself. $$
{\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b} =
\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
{\mathbf i} & {\mathbf j}&{\mathbf k}\\
a_1 & a_2 &a_3\\
b_1 & b_2 &b_3
\end{array}
\right|
= {\mathbf i}
\left|
\begin{array}{cc}
a_2 &a_3\\
b_2 &b_3
\end{array}
\right|
+ {\mathbf j}
\left|
\begin{array}{cc}
a_3 & a_1\\
b_3 & b_1
\end{array}
\right|
+ {\mathbf k}
\left|
\begin{array}{cc}
a_1 & a_2\\
b_1 & b_2
\end{array}
\right|
$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Remark** In these notes we define the vector product geometrically and go on to deduce the component form. Anton first defines the vector product using the determinant ( and then deduces the geometric properties. Either approach is good. But I would advise you to get familiar with the vector form as it will make calculations much simpler and quicker later on.\`

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.8 The Scalar Triple Product

We saw earlier that if ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b}$ are two vectors, then the **area** of the parallelogram spanned by them is given by the magnitude of ${\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}$. Now consider *three* vectors ${\mathbf a},{\mathbf b}, {\mathbf c}$. These can be thought of as the sides of a parallolopiped (think of a squashed cube). The scalar triple product allows us to calculate the **volume** of this solid object.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Definition 2.18**

> Given three vectors ${\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}$, their **scalar triple product**, denoted by $[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}]$, is the scalar

> $$[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}] := {\mathbf a}. ({\mathbf b}\times {\mathbf c})$$

**The component form of the scalar triple product:**

$$[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}]  = a_1({\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf c})_1 + a_2({\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf c})_2 +
a_3({\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf c})_3 $$

$$= a_1(b_2 c_3 - b_3 c_2) + a_2 (b_3c_1 - b_1c_3) + a_3 (b_1 c_2
- b_2c_1)$$

$$= \left|\begin{array}{ccc} a_1 &a_2 &a_3\\ 
b_1 &b_2 &b_3\\
c_1   &c_2 &c_3 
\end{array}\right|$$ - the $3 \times 3$ determinant again!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Back to the geometric interpretation:**

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot29, out.width='40%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig29.jpg")
```

\noindent Consider the parallelepiped $\cal{P}$ (spanned by ${\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}, {\mathbf c}$). The area of the base is $\|{\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf c}\|$. The height is $\|{\mathbf a}\| \cos(\theta)$ if $(0 \le \theta \le \frac{\pi}{2}),$ or $-\|{\mathbf a}\| \cos(\theta)$ if $(\frac{\pi}{2} \le \theta \le \pi)$. (Here $\theta$ is the angle between ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf c}$.) If the volume of $\cal{P}$ is denoted by $V$, then $$
[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}] =  V >0,\;\quad \mbox{if}\; {\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c} \;\mbox{is right handed}$$

$$[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}] = -V<0,\; \quad \mbox{if}\;{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b}, {\mathbf c} \;\mbox{is left handed.}$$ \noindent So $[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}]$ is a *signed* volume of a parallelepiped.

\noindent Since the volume of the parallelepiped as well as the right-handedness property are unchanged if the vectors ${\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}$ and ${\mathbf c}$ are interchanged cyclically we see immediately that $$
 {\mathbf a}. ({\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf c}) =  {\mathbf b}. ({\mathbf c} \times {\mathbf a}) =  {\mathbf c}. ({\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}).
$$ \noindent Here we have kept the $.$ and the $\times$ fixed and cyclically interchanged ${\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}$ and ${\mathbf c}$. We give a full list of the properties of the scalar triple product shortly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**This result will become insanely important when we want to change variables in multi-variate calculus!**

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Co-planar vectors:**

Three vectors are **co-planar** (in other words they all lie in the same plane) if there exist scalars $\lambda, \mu, \nu,\; \mbox{with}\;
\lambda^2 + \mu^2 +\nu^2 > 0,\; \mbox{such that}\; \lambda {\mathbf a} + \mu {\mathbf b} + \nu {\mathbf c} = {\mathbf 0}$. We say that ${\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}$ and ${\mathbf c}$ are *linearly dependent* vectors.

$$
[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}] = 0 \iff {\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c} \quad \mbox{are co-planar }\,.
$$ **Exercise** The proof of this result follows immediately from the geometric interpretation. Make sure that you understand why.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Properties of the scalar triple product**

-   [1] $$[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}]= [{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}, {\mathbf a}] = [{\mathbf c},{\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}] $$ $$= -[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf c},{\mathbf b}] = -[{\mathbf b},{\mathbf a},{\mathbf c}]= -[{\mathbf c},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf a}]$$

Setting ${\mathbf c}={\mathbf a}$ gives $$[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf a}] = 0, \quad 
\forall {\mathbf a},{\mathbf b}$$

-   [2] $[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}+{\mathbf d}] = [{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}] + [{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf d}]$

-   [3] $\lambda [{\mathbf a},{\mathbf b},{\mathbf c}] = [\lambda {\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}, {\mathbf c}]$

Properties (1) - (3) follow from the properties of the scalar and the vector products.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Example:** $$
[{\mathbf i},{\mathbf j},{\mathbf k}] = {\mathbf i} .({\mathbf j} \times {\mathbf k}) = {\mathbf i}. {\mathbf i} = 1.
$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We can now answer my Cambridge Entrance question:

**Proof of the distributive law, property (2), for the vector product:**

We wish to prove: $$
{\mathbf a} \times({\mathbf b}+{\mathbf c})= {\mathbf a}\times {\mathbf b} + {\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf c}.
$$

**Proof** To prove this result (which is hard - as I found! - to prove straight from the definitions), we use the cyclic property of the scalar triple product (twice) and the distributive property of the scalar product.

Let ${\mathbf x}$ be an arbitrary vector and then consider

\begin{eqnarray*} 
{\mathbf x}.{\mathbf a} \times ({\mathbf b}+{\mathbf c}) & = & ({\mathbf b}+{\mathbf c}).{\mathbf x} \times {\mathbf a} \quad \mbox{(cyclic STP)}\\
& = & {\mathbf b}.{\mathbf x} \times {\mathbf a}+ {\mathbf c}. {\mathbf x} \times {\mathbf a} \quad \mbox{(distributive property of scalar product)}\\
& = & {\mathbf x}. {\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b} + {\mathbf x}.{\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf c} \quad \mbox{(cyclic STP)}\\
& = & {\mathbf x}. ( {\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b} + {\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf c}).
\end{eqnarray*} Therefore $$
 {\mathbf x}. ( {\mathbf a}\times({\mathbf b}+{\mathbf c}))\,=\,  {\mathbf x}.( {\mathbf a}\times {\mathbf b} + {\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf c})),
$$ for **all** ${\mathbf x}$. Corollary 2.15 then gives us the result that $$
{\mathbf a}\times({\mathbf b}+{\mathbf c})= {\mathbf a}\times {\mathbf b} + {\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf c},
$$ as required.$\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.9 The Triple Vector Product

Now we have defined the scalar triple product it is natural to consider what we might mean by the **vector triple product**. In fact we have two **vector triple products:** defined by

> $${\mathbf a} \times ({\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf c}) = ({\mathbf c}.{\mathbf a}) \; {\mathbf b} - ({\mathbf b}. {\mathbf a}) \; {\mathbf c} \quad \mbox{and} \quad 
> ({\mathbf a}\times {\mathbf b}) \times {\mathbf c} = ({\mathbf a} . {\mathbf c}) \; {\mathbf b} - ({\mathbf b}. {\mathbf c}) \; {\mathbf a} $$

**NOTE** These two vector triple products are NOT the same. For those of you who like group theory, the cross product is *not* associative. However it does define what is called an *Algebra*.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

How to remember these identities for your exam? (Which you need to do!) One way is note that each of the vectors inside the brackets on the left appears once outside the brackets on the right and the middle' vector ${\mathbf b}$ appears first. Each term contains ${\mathbf a}, {\mathbf b}, {\mathbf c}$ once only.

Another way is to used the mnemonic **CAB - BAC** for the first identity.

Think of sitting in the back of a taxi to help remember this. *I once shared the back of a taxi with Carol Vorderman, but that is another story.*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Proof of the identity** ${\mathbf a} \times ({\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf a}) = ({\mathbf c} . {\mathbf a}) \; {\mathbf b} - ({\mathbf b}.{\mathbf a}) \; {\mathbf c}$.

We use components. First, if ${\mathbf a} = {\mathbf 0}$ then the result is true. Assume ${\mathbf a} \ne {\mathbf 0}$, and select the axes such that ${\mathbf a} = a {\mathbf i}$.

$$LHS = a  \;{\mathbf i} \times \{ (b_2c_3 - b_3c_2) {\mathbf i} + (b_3c_1 - b_1 c_3) {\mathbf j} + (b_1c_2 - b_2 c_1) {\mathbf k} \} 
= (- a(b_1c_2 - b_2c_1)) {\mathbf j} + (a(b_3c_1 - b_1c_3)) {\mathbf k} $$ $$RHS = (a {\mathbf i}.{\mathbf c}) {\mathbf b} - (a {\mathbf i}.{\mathbf b}) {\mathbf c}= (ac_1) {\mathbf b}- (ab_1) {\mathbf c}$$ $$ = (a c_1)(b_1 {\mathbf i} +b_2 {\mathbf j} +b_3 {\mathbf k}) - (a b_1)(c_1 {\mathbf i}+c_2 {\mathbf j}+c_3 {\mathbf k})$$ $$=  a (c_1b_2 - c_2b_1) {\mathbf j} +  a(c_1b_3 - c_3b_1) {\mathbf k} = LHS.$$ 

The equivalent identity for the second vector triple product immediately follows: $$
({\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}) \times {\mathbf c} = - {\mathbf c} \times ({\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}) = 
- \left\{({\mathbf c}. {\mathbf b}) {\mathbf a} - ({\mathbf c} . {\mathbf a}) {\mathbf b} \right\}\,=\,
({\mathbf a} . {\mathbf c}) {\mathbf b} - ({\mathbf b}. {\mathbf c}) {\mathbf a}. 
$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Important Exercise** (you should do this, if only for the real pleasure in seeing a lovely result):}

Prove the *beautiful* **Jacobi identity:**

> $${\mathbf a} \times ({\mathbf b} \times {\mathbf c}) + {\mathbf b} \times ({\mathbf c} \times {\mathbf a}) + {\mathbf c} \times
> ({\mathbf a} \times {\mathbf b}) = {\mathbf 0}$$

\noindent {\\bf Hint} Expand out the 3 vector triple products.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

\noindent NOTE In the third year of your course (should you choose to do so) we will generalise all of this lovely stuff when we look at {\em differential geometry} in general and {\em Lie Algebras} in particular.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.10 Summary

In this Chapter the main tools for manipulating vectors have been defined and discussed. These tools are, the dot product, the vector product, the scalar triple product and the vector triple product. We shall see how these are used in geometry, in kinematics (especially rotational motion) and in mechanics (where we will bend it like Beckham), in the following Chapters.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Chapter 3: Straight lines and planes

In this Chapter we will put the theory of vectors to work, to allow us to represent, and do calculations with, lines and planes and some other surfaces in 3-D. In particular we derive equations for these. We shall answer some typical questions in 3-D geometry, like `what is the equation of the common perpendicular to two given lines'', and`find the perpendicular distance from a point to a plane'' and "when does a line intersect a plane". These questions are not only interesting and important in their own right, but they lie at the heart of the modern computer graphics industry. For more information on this see my article *Maths goes to the movies* on Moodle.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

In this Chapter we will start by looking at lines, then we will look at planes. In the next section we will look at some more exotic surfaces which may change with time.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3.1 The equation of a straight line.

Perhaps the simplest geometrical concept (after a point) is that of a straight line. One application of straight lines is in optics, and finding the intersection of straight lines with objects is used in the graphics industry to see how those objects are illuminated by light. To work with lines, we need to know their equations. First we find the equation of a straight line.

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot131, out.width='60%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig31.jpg")
```

A line $L$ in $R^3$ through a point $A$, is uniquely specified by the choice of the point $A$ and a direction vector ${\mathbf l} \ne
{\mathbf 0}$. Let $A$ have position vector ${\mathbf a}$. Then a point $R$ with position vector ${\mathbf r}$ is on the line if and only if there exists $\lambda \in R$, such that ${\mathbf r} = {\mathbf a} + \lambda {\mathbf l}$. The **vector equation** of the line is given by taking all values of $\lambda$ so that

> $${\mathbf r} = {\mathbf a} + \lambda {\mathbf l}, \quad(-\infty < \lambda <
> + \infty)\;.\quad \quad (3.1)$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> **Definition 3.1**

> Equation (3.1) is the parametric form of the vector equation of a straight line. As the real parameter' $\lambda$ varies from $-\infty$ to $+ \infty,$ the point $R$ with position vector ${\mathbf r}$ traces out the entire line.

The **component form** of (3.1) is as follows. For $$
{\mathbf r} = (x,y,z), \quad
  {\mathbf a} =(a_1,a_2,a_3), \quad {\mathbf l} = (l_1,l_2,l_3)
$$

then the line $L$ is given by

$$L = \{ (x,y,z): x = a_1 + \lambda l_1, y = a_2 + \lambda l_2, z = a_3 + \lambda l_3 \}$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

An **alternative** and often very useful form} of the equation of a straight line is as follows. The vector $\overrightarrow{AR}$ is parallel to ${\mathbf l}$ if and only if

> $$ ({\mathbf r} -{\mathbf a}) \times {\mathbf l} = {\mathbf 0} \quad \quad (3.2) $$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We now give several examples which illustrate the use of equations (3.1), (3.2).

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Example:** Find the vector equation of the line passing through the points $A$ and $B$ with position vectors ${\mathbf a} = {\mathbf i} +
{\mathbf j},\; {\mathbf b} = {\mathbf j} + {\mathbf k}$ respectively.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Solution:** Now ${\mathbf l} = {\mathbf b} - {\mathbf a} = {\mathbf k} - {\mathbf i}$, and using the formula ${\mathbf r} = {\mathbf a} + \lambda {\mathbf l}$, we obtain $$
 {\mathbf r} = {\mathbf i} + {\mathbf j} + \lambda ({\mathbf k} - {\mathbf i}).
$$

$$
x = 1 - \lambda,\, y = 1,\, z = \lambda, \quad \quad (\mbox{or } y =
1,\, x = 1 - z,\, z \mbox{ is arbitrary}). \quad \Box
$$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Exercise** Use the alternative form of the equation of the line given by (3.2) to obtain the equation of the line in the previous example.

[Hint: $({\mathbf r}-{\mathbf a}) \times {\mathbf l} = {\mathbf 0}$ implies $$
({\mathbf r}-{\mathbf i}-{\mathbf j}) \times ({\mathbf k}-{\mathbf i}) = {\mathbf 0}.
$$ Now, with ${\mathbf r}=(x,y,z)$, apply the determinant form of the cross product.] $\quad \Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We now consider two important geometrical questions which provide very useful results later on in this Chapter and are are also useful in computer animation applications when we want to see how objects move around, and even in Air Traffic Control.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Find the **condition that two lines intersect**. (For an air traffic contoller, this will tell them if two aircraft might crash into each other). Given two non-parallel lines in $R^3$ $$
L_1 : {\mathbf r} = {\mathbf a} + \lambda  \; {\mathbf l}, \quad \lambda \in R$$ $$L_2 : {\mathbf r} = {\mathbf b} + \mu \; {\mathbf m}, \quad \mu \in R,$$ show that they intersect if and only if

> $$[{\mathbf a}, {\mathbf l}, {\mathbf m}] = [{\mathbf b}, {\mathbf l}, {\mathbf m}]\; \quad \quad (3.3) 
> $$

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot132, out.width='60%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig32.jpg")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Solution:** From the figure it is clear that if the point $A$, with position vector ${\mathbf a}$, is on $L_1$ and $B$, with position vector ${\mathbf b}$ is on $L_2$, and there is a point $P$ on the intersection of the two lines so that $P\in L_1 \cap
L_2$ then the vectors $({\mathbf a} - {\mathbf b}), {\mathbf l}, {\mathbf m}$ are co-planar. Thus $[{\mathbf a} - {\mathbf b}, {\mathbf l}, {\mathbf m}] = 0$ Hence $[{\mathbf a},
{\mathbf l}, {\mathbf m}] = [{\mathbf b}, {\mathbf l}, {\mathbf m}]$, using properties of the triple scalar product. $\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We will now think of a problem faced by an air traffic controller (and by the pilots of the aircraft!). You have two aircraft travelling on straight line paths $L_1$ and $L_2$. How close will they get to each other?

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot1Xz, out.width='40%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Xz3sD.jpg")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

To do this calculation we need to work out the distance between the two lines. We do this by calculating the line which is a *common perpendicular* to both lines, and then working out the length of this.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

*Problem:* Let $$L_1 : {\mathbf r} =  {\mathbf a} + \lambda {\mathbf l}$$ $$L_2 : {\mathbf r} = {\mathbf b} + \mu {\mathbf m}$$

be two non-intersecting, non-parallel lines in $R^3$. What is the equation of the common perpendicular $L_{\bot}$?

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot133, out.width='60%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig33.jpg")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

*Solution:* We seek $L_\bot : {\mathbf r} = {\mathbf c} + \nu {\mathbf n}$ for some direction vector ${\mathbf n}$. Now $L_{\bot} \bot L_1$ and $L_{\bot} \bot L_2$. Therefore we can take ${\mathbf n} := {\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf m}$.

Take $C$ to be the point of intersection of $L_2 \cap
L_{\bot}$. Since $C \in L_2$, there exists a real $\mu_0$ such that $${\mathbf c} = {\mathbf b} + \mu_0 {\mathbf m}.$$

Therefore $$
L_{\bot}: {\mathbf r} = {\mathbf b} + \mu_0 {\mathbf m}
+ \nu ({\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf m}).
$$ Now we need to determine $\mu_0$. To do this we use the fact that $L_\bot$ also intersects $L_1$, and so, using the result in (3.3), $$
[{\mathbf a},{\mathbf l},{\mathbf n}] = [{\mathbf c},{\mathbf l},{\mathbf n}] = [{\mathbf b}+\mu_0 {\mathbf m},{\mathbf l},{\mathbf n}].
$$

*(Make sure you understand why this is so.)*

Thus $$
[{\mathbf a},\, {\mathbf l},\, {\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf m}] = [{\mathbf b} + \mu_0 {\mathbf m},\, {\mathbf l},\, {\mathbf l} \times
{\mathbf m}].
$$

Therefore $$
\mu_0 = \frac{[{\mathbf a} - {\mathbf b},\, {\mathbf l},\, {\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf m}]}{[{\mathbf m},\, {\mathbf l},\, {\mathbf l}
\times {\mathbf m}]}.
$$ Note that the denominator is $$
[{\mathbf m}, {\mathbf l}, {\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf m}]=[{\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf m}, {\mathbf m},{\mathbf l}]=
({\mathbf l}
\times {\mathbf m}). ({\mathbf m} \times {\mathbf l}) = -({\mathbf l}
\times {\mathbf m}). ({\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf m}) = -\|{\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf m}\|^2,
$$ which is nonzero since the lines are non-parallel (hence ${\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf n} \neq {\mathbf 0}$). $\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We can also find the point $D$ with vector ${\mathbf d}$ where the perpendicular $L_{\perp}$ intersects the line $L_1$. We will have $${\mathbf d} = {\mathbf a} + \lambda_0 {\mathbf l}.$$ We can find the value of $\lambda_0$ by interchanging the two lines in the expression for $\mu_0$. This gives $$
\lambda_0 = \frac{[{\mathbf b} - {\mathbf a},\, {\mathbf m},\, {\mathbf m} \times {\mathbf l}]}{[{\mathbf l},\, {\mathbf m},\, {\mathbf m}
\times {\mathbf l}]}.
$$

Now we have found the points $C$ and $D$ the length of the shortest line between $L_1$ and $L_2$ is given by $\| {\mathbf c} - {\mathbf d} \|$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

\noindent NOTE Distances between lines, and between lines and points, is now an important aspect of the rapidly growing field of machine learning. This is because we use lines and planes to separate different types of data and to sort it into subsets, such as cats and dogs.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3.4 The equation of the plane

A plane is the set of points which lie on a flat surface. We usually call a plane a two-dimensional surface.A lthough we live on a round Earth, because we are small in comparison we experience it as a plane. (Of course if you believe in a flat Earth then it *is* a plane.) In computer graphics we often represent a complicated shape as a set of intersecting planes and look at the way that light reflects from them. All of this makes it worth studying the plane in some detail.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

There are several ways that we can represent a plane. In general we will find that it is the set of points $(x,y,z)$ such that $$a x + b y + cz + d = 0,$$ where $a,b,c$ and $d$ are constants.

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot135, out.width='60%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig35.jpg")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Let $\Pi$ be a plane. It can be specified by a point $A$ on the plane with position vector ${\mathbf a}$, and two *non-parallel* vectors ${\mathbf l}$ and ${\mathbf m}$ with in the plane $\Pi$. We say ${\mathbf l}$ and ${\mathbf m}$ are parallel to $\Pi$. Then for any point $R \in \Pi$ with position vector ${\mathbf r}$ there are a unique pair of *scalars* $\lambda$ and $\mu$ such that

> $${\mathbf r} = {\mathbf a} + \lambda {\mathbf l} + \mu {\mathbf m}, \quad (3.4) $$

Equation (3.4) is the *parametric* form of the vector equation of the plane.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Alternative form:** There is an alternative, and much more useful, form for the equation of a plane is to think of it as all of the points orthogonal to a given vector. To describe this, let ${\mathbf N}$ be a vector *perpendicular* to $\Pi$ (a **normal** to $\Pi$). For example, one such vector is given by $$
 {\mathbf N} = {\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf m}
$$ for the above ${\mathbf l}, {\mathbf m}$. Now let ${\mathbf a}$ be a fixed point in the plane, and $R$ a general point. Then, $R \in \Pi \Leftrightarrow$

> $$({\mathbf r} - {\mathbf a}). {\mathbf N}= 0. \quad (3.5) $$

We can re-write (3.5) as ${\mathbf r}. {\mathbf N} = {\mathbf a}. {\mathbf N} =
D$, say. In components with $${\mathbf N} = (A,B,C),\quad \mbox{and } \quad 
{\mathbf r} = (x,y,z),$$ then

> $$A \; x + B \; y
> +C \; z = D \;. \quad (3.6)$$

\vspace{0.1in}

**Example:** Find the equation of the plane passing through $A=(1,2,3)$ and perpendicular to ${\mathbf N} =(0,1,1)$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Solution:** Since ${\mathbf a}.{\mathbf N}=5$ we have ${\mathbf r}.{\mathbf N}={\mathbf a}.{\mathbf N}=5$. Therefore the equation of the plane is $$
y+z=5.
$$$\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

A special case is when ${\mathbf N}$ is a **unit** normal, which we denote by ${\mathbf n}$. Then we have

$$({\mathbf r} - {\mathbf a}) \cdot {\mathbf n} = 0  \quad (3.6)$$ In terms of the above ${\mathbf l}, {\mathbf m}$, we can take the unit normal to be $$
{\mathbf n}= \pm \, \frac{{\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf m}}{\|{\mathbf l} \times {\mathbf m}\|} \cdot
$$

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot136, out.width='60%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig36.jpg")
```

Note that equation (3.6) may also be written

> $${\mathbf r}. {\mathbf n} = d   \quad (3.7) $$ with $d := {\mathbf a}. {\mathbf n}$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The number $d$ in the above formula has a special geometric meaning. To see this, let $R \in \Pi$ be a point in the plane, with position vector ${\mathbf r}$ so that ${\mathbf r}$ is orthogonal to the plane, and thus ${\mathbf r}$ is parallel to ${\mathbf n}$. It follows that ${\mathbf r}= \lambda {\mathbf n}$ with $\lambda = \pm \|r\|$. So $$
d={\mathbf r}.{\mathbf n} = \lambda {\mathbf n}.{\mathbf n}=\lambda= \pm \| r \|.
$$ Hence $d$ is $\pm$ the **perpendicular distance** from $O$ to $\Pi$. $\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

The component form of (3.7) is, with ${\mathbf n} = (n_1, n_2,n_3)$, $$ n_1\;x + n_2\;y + n_3\; z = d\;.\quad (3.8) $$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

> Let us now consider some examples.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Example 1:** Let $\Pi$ be the plane given by $x + 3y + 4z = -2$. What is the perpendicular distance from $O$ to $\Pi$?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Solution:** From the equation of the plane we see that the normal ${\mathbf N}$ is given by $$
{\mathbf N} = (1, 3, 4),
$$ and the unit normal is $$
{\mathbf n} = \frac{{\mathbf N}}{\|{\mathbf N}\|} = \frac{{\mathbf N}}{\sqrt{26}}.
$$ Hence, $$
{\mathbf r} \cdot {\mathbf n} = \frac{{\mathbf r} \cdot {\mathbf N}}{\sqrt{26}} =
-\,\frac{2}{\sqrt{26}}
$$ Thus, the distance from $O$ to $\Pi$ is $\frac{2}{\sqrt{26}}$. $\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Example 2:** Find the intersection of a line $$
L : {\mathbf r} = {\mathbf a} + \lambda {\mathbf l},\, \lambda \in R
$$ and a plane $$
\Pi :\, {\mathbf r}. {\mathbf N} = D.
$$ \noindent Let $S$ be the point of intersection, with position vector ${\mathbf s}={\mathbf a} + \lambda_0 {\mathbf l}$. (Draw a diagram here if you wish.) Now $S$ lies both on the line and in the plane, so $$
({\mathbf a} + \lambda_0 {\mathbf l}). {\mathbf N} = D\,\,\, \Rightarrow\,\,\, \lambda_0 =
\frac{D - {\mathbf a} . {\mathbf N}}{{\mathbf l}. {\mathbf N}}.
$$ $\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Example 3:** Find the perpendicular distance between the point $B$ with position vector ${\mathbf b}$ and the plane $\Pi : {\mathbf r}. {\mathbf N} = D$.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Solution:** Let the perpendicular distance be $h$.

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot137, out.width='60%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig37.jpg")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Draw the perpendicular from B to $\Pi$ and let it meet $\Pi$ at $B'$. Thus, $\overrightarrow{BB'}\; \bot\; \Pi$. Therefore $\overrightarrow{BB'}\; \|\; {\mathbf N}$, and so $$
\overrightarrow{BB'} = \lambda_0 \; {\mathbf N},\; \mbox{for some } \lambda_0 \in R.
$$

\noindent Then $({\mathbf b} + \lambda_0 {\mathbf N})$ is the position vector of $B'$. Hence $$
 ({\mathbf b}+ \lambda_0 {\mathbf N}) \cdot {\mathbf N} = D.
$$ \noindent So ${\mathbf b}.{\mathbf N} + \lambda_0\|{\mathbf N}\|^2 = D$, and hence $$
\lambda_0\,
=\, \frac{D - {\mathbf b} \cdot {\mathbf N}}{\|{\mathbf N}\|^2}.
$$

Therefore, \> $$h = \|\overrightarrow{BB'}\| = |\lambda_0|\;\|{\mathbf N}\| =
\frac{|D - {\mathbf b}. {\mathbf N}|}{\|{\mathbf N}\|}.$$. $\Box$

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Summary

In this Chapter we have derived the basic equations of a straight line and a plane in 3-D . In addition, several useful results were obtained, for example, (3.3) gives a condition for two lines to intersect (which is useful in air traffic contriol and also in computer graphics). This result was used to obtain the equation of the common perpendicular to two straight lines. Planes and normals go hand in hand, see (3.5) and (3.7). Important techniques to learn and remember are how to find the normal to a plane, and how to find the perpendicular distance from a point to a plane. These will all come in handy later when we look at how objects move around.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

------------------------------------------------------------------------




# Chapter 4: Vector functions, line integrals and directional derivatives.



Whilst lines and planes are very important in geometry, real life is full of much more exotic shapes. Fortunately, vector calculus gives us a way of representing these, and also seeing how they might change. This is vital information if you are trying to represent an image in a computer graphics simulation, or to plot the path of a space craft or an aircraft. In this Chapter we will show how we can do this. We will start by looking at general parametric curves. That is, curves which are described by a parameter (usually the variable $t$). We will then look at what happens when we differentiate these with respect to $t$ to find velocities and accelerations. We will look at integrating with respect to $t$. This allows us to work out quantities such as energy.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 4.1 Examples of parametric curves in 3-D

```{r echo=FALSE, ho-plot141, out.width='60%', fig.show='hold', fig.cap=""}
knitr::include_graphics("Fig41.jpg")
```

Let $P= (x(t),y(t),z(t))$ be a point whose position vector ${\mathbf r}$ varies with \`\`time" $t$, so that, $$
{\mathbf r} = {\mathbf r}(t) = x(t) \; {\mathbf i} + y(t) \; {\mathbf j} + z(t) \; {\mathbf k}.
\quad (4.1)$$ The components $x(t),\, y(t),\, z(t)$ are real-valued (scalar) functions of the real variable $t$. So, a vector-valued function ${\mathbf r}(t)$ may be interpreted as a **triple** of real-valued functions. As $t$ varies, the point $P$ traces out a curve C.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Example 1:** *The straight line* If ${\mathbf a}$ and ${\mathbf l}$ are constant vectors then ${\mathbf r}(t) = {\mathbf a} + t {\mathbf l}$ represents the equation of a straight line, $L$ say.
